title: The Tulsa 'Race Riots'
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre (also called the Tulsa Race Riot), prompted by HBO's Watchmen bringing attention to it. They cover Greenwood, the prosperous Black district known as Black Wall Street; the Dick Rowland and Sarah Page elevator incident; the Tulsa Tribune's inflammatory headlines and editorial; the sheriff McCullough standoff with armed Black World War One veterans; the shooting that set off the violence; the coordinated white assault on Greenwood, arson, and attacks by air; the National Guard's role in arresting Black residents; the death toll debate; the insurance classification as a riot; the rebuilding; mass graves; and the late-1990s and later efforts at acknowledgment. The episode closes with listener mail about the pronunciation of Carrie Elwes's... specifically the pronunciation of Eli's name and a correction-corner apology.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the Tulsa massacre
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck return from a break, chat about coffee, and bring up HBO's Watchmen as the reason the Tulsa massacre is in the news. They frame the event as a buried episode of history.

segments.title: Greenwood: Black Wall Street
segments.summary: Greenwood, an affluent all-Black district north of Tulsa, is described with its businesses, wealth, and institutions. Its prosperity is traced to Oklahoma's Jim Crow laws and the community's self-reliance.

segments.title: Racial violence across the United States in 1919 and after
segments.summary: The hosts note that similar race riots and lynchings happened elsewhere, including in 1919 in Chicago, Washington D.C., and St. Louis, and that the aim of the mob was a lynching. Oklahoma's ties to the South and West are discussed.

segments.title: Dick Rowland and the elevator incident with Sarah Page
segments.summary: Dick Rowland, a shoeshine boy, and Sarah Page, a white elevator operator at the Drexel Building, are introduced. Accounts differ on why Rowland was in the elevator. The hosts describe the alleged stumble and the cry of assault, and note how little is known about either person.

segments.title: Tulsa Tribune headlines and the white crowd at the courthouse
segments.summary: The Tulsa Tribune published an inflammatory article and an editorial calling for a lynching. A white crowd gathered at the courthouse demanding Rowland. Sheriff William McCullough refused to hand him over.

segments.title: Black World War One veterans confront the mob
segments.summary: Armed Black World War One veterans from Greenwood came to the courthouse to protect Rowland. The hosts describe their earlier denial from the Memorial Day parade. About seventy-five armed men showed up.

segments.title: The gunshot that started the violence and the assault on Greenwood
segments.summary: An older white man tried to take a veteran's gun, the gun went off, and shooting broke out. Sheriff McCullough deputized white rioters and handed out weapons. A coordinated white assault on Greenwood followed, with homes and businesses set on fire and people killed.

segments.title: Destruction of Greenwood, National Guard, and death toll
segments.summary: Thirty-five blocks were burned, including the homes of A.C. Jackson, churches, schools, and businesses. Planes were used to drop incendiaries. The National Guard arrested Black residents. Death toll estimates vary from thirty-five officially to as many as three hundred.

segments.title: Aftermath, rebuilding, and later acknowledgment
segments.summary: Survivors were detained at the fairgrounds and released when white employers vouched for them. No one was prosecuted, insurers classed the event as a riot, and rebuilding followed. Mass graves were later found. The state did not acknowledge the event until the late 1990s, and the Tulsa Race Riot Commission reported in 2001. Listener mail about the pronunciation of Eli's name closes the episode.
